scenes.title: The house by the Junction
scenes.intro: Henry grew up at Stoford, on the edge of Yeovil, in a small terraced house by Yeovil Junction railway station. He was the eldest of twelve children.

context.text: "How you got 14 people into that house I will never know."
The railway reached Stoford in 1860, cutting the old village in half, and Yeovil Junction station gave work to local men.

paras: Found this old book in the drawer today, under the King's letter. I'd not looked at it in forty years. I said I'd never write in it again, and here I am with a pencil, like an old fool.

There's a photograph on the dresser of all of us, Mother and Father and the twelve of us, grown, outside the old house by the Junction. I look at it and I see the boy I was before any of it. He didn't know anything. Lucky lad.
The grandchildren ask what Grandad did in the war. I tell them to mind their manners and eat their dinner.
Some things you put away. But I'll write a little here, where nobody will read it. I owe it to the lads who never got old.
basis: A family photograph shows Henry's parents and their twelve grown-up children outside the house at Yeovil Junction. Henry kept the King's letter given to returning prisoners (family memories; the letter itself is still to be found).
He "never talked to anybody about the War" (Grandma Angela's memoir).
The notebook is imagined. These later entries are in an older voice, written as if Henry opened it again near the end of his life.

paras: Harvest's late this year and every hand is wanted, so I'm in the fields from first light till you can't see the stooks. Came home tonight with my arms scratched to ribbons and my back like an old man's.

Fourteen of us in that little house now, counting Mother and Father. You can't turn round without treading on somebody. The little ones sleep three to a bed and the trains go by the bottom of the garden all night, and none of us hears them any more.

But tonight the trains were different. Train after train going through the Junction, and men on the platform saying it's war. Germany. Nobody seems to know rightly what it's about, only that we're in it now, and the papers say it'll be over by Christmas.
Mother says it's nothing to do with us. Father says it's everything to do with us. I said nothing and went to bed, and lay there listening to the trains.
basis: His parents lived in "a small terraced house out by Yeovil Junction Railway Station, Stoford". Grandma Angela's memoir says: "How you got 14 people into that house I will never know." Henry was the eldest of twelve and worked as a farm hand.
Henry was born on 14 June 1894, so he was 20 when war broke out (his birth certificate).
Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914, in the middle of the harvest.
His father, Arthur Bowles, was a farm labourer, and was still digging ditches at 90 (Memories of Grandad).
The harvest, the trains, and what his parents said.

scenes.title: The eldest of twelve
scenes.intro: Most of what we know about Henry's early life comes from what his granddaughter, Angela Wright, remembers and wrote down. These are her words.

stories.title: Henry, or Harry
stories.quote: Henry Bowles (or Harry as some knew him)
stories.body: At home and in the army he was Henry John Bowles. To many people he was Harry.

stories.title: Twelve children
stories.body: Henry was the eldest child of Arthur Bowles and his wife. They lived into their nineties, in the same small house by Yeovil Junction station.
stories.quote: the eldest of 12 children who all survived WWI

stories.title: The twelve
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright; the family photograph; newspaper cutting, December 1953
stories.body: Henry was the eldest. His brothers and sisters were Reg, Winnie, Frank, George, Ethel, Arthur, Amy, Lilly, Bill, Kit and Oliver, the youngest. Their mother was Eliza Ann Bowles. Her maiden name is still to be found.

stories.title: Born near Glastonbury
stories.body: Henry was born on 14 June 1894. His birth was registered in the Glastonbury sub-district of Wells, in the middle of Somerset, so the family only moved to Stoford, near Yeovil, later. Exactly where he was born, and when they moved, is still to be found.

stories.title: Sixty years married
stories.body: Arthur and Eliza Ann Bowles married on 27 December 1893, and celebrated their diamond wedding in December 1953 with a party at the R.A.O.B. Club in Yeovil: the Buffaloes, the same order Henry belonged to. They had seven sons, five daughters, 32 grandchildren and 14 great-grandchildren. The eldest of the family was 59: that was Henry. Only one of them had died, the eldest grandson Gilbert, Henry's son.

stories.title: Six oxen
stories.body: At 87, Arthur had done every job on a farm except drive a tractor, and remembered ploughing with a team of six oxen. A fortnight before the party he had laid a hedge untouched for thirty years. When they married he earned ten shillings a week, and Eliza Ann £7 a year in service.
stories.who: Arthur Bowles, on ploughing with oxen

stories.title: Bright as a button
stories.body: At 82, Eliza Ann still took the train into Yeovil to shop two or three times a week, and did all her own washing. She had met Arthur when she was 16.
stories.quote: I look after Grandpa, and he looks after me.

stories.title: Granfy Bowles
stories.body: Henry's father Arthur was a farm labourer all his life.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: there is a newspaper report of him still digging ditches at the age of 90
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Keeping them in line
stories.body: He did not like rudeness or bad language, especially in front of women and children, and he told his brothers and sisters so, even when they were grown up. Some of them, the family only visited now and then.
stories.quote: would often reprimand his siblings for their behaviour, right into their adult life

stories.title: On the land
stories.body: Henry worked as a farm hand. A family photograph from about 1920 shows him on a horse-drawn mower behind two heavy horses, with his baby son Gilbert on his lap (Chapter 7).

photos.caption: Arthur Bowles and his wife with all twelve of their children, outside the family's terraced house by Yeovil Junction station, in the 1920s. Back row, left to right: Arthur, Ethel, George, Frank, Winnie and Reg. Middle row, left to right: Bill, Lilly, their father Arthur, their mother, Amy and Henry, the eldest, on the far right. On the step: Kit and Oliver, the youngest.
photos.alt: A large family group of eighteen people in 1920s clothes in front of two numbered front doors of a brick terrace. An older couple sit in the middle, surrounded by their grown-up sons and daughters, with a young woman and a boy sitting on the step in front.

photos.docName: Newspaper cutting, He Ploughed With Six Oxen
photos.caption: A local newspaper cutting from December 1953, kept by the family: Henry's parents, Arthur and Eliza Ann Bowles, celebrate sixty years of marriage. The paper's name and date were cut off.
photos.alt: A yellowed newspaper cutting with the headline He Ploughed With Six Oxen. A full transcript follows.
photos.credit: Newspaper cutting kept by the family
transcript: A family of 60, one for each of 60 years of happy marriage, will celebrate a diamond wedding at a Yeovil party on Saturday.
Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Bowles, of 7, Hillside View, Stoford, married on December 27 1893, have seven sons, five daughters, 32 grandchildren and 14 great-grandchildren.

All but one of the family, Mr. Bill Bowles, of Yeovil, ill in hospital, will be at the party at the R.A.O.B. Club. Their ages range from 59 to a few days: the youngest grandchild was born on Christmas Eve.
Mr. Bowles, 87 on Christmas Day, has been a farm-worker all his life. He has done every job on a farm except drive a tractor, and he remembers ploughing with a team of six oxen: "better than horses."
Wiry and tough, he still does odd jobs for local farmers. A fortnight ago he laid a hedge that had been untouched for 30 years.
Mrs. Eliza Ann Bowles, 82 on December 18, is still bright as a button. She takes the train into Yeovil two or three times a week to go shopping, does all her own washing, and cleans her own house.
She met her husband when she was 16. When they married, five years later, she earned £7 a year in service, and he earned 10s. a week.
In their 60 years together only one member of the family has died: Gilbert, the eldest grandson, six years ago.
How to be healthy and happy together for 60 years? Hard work, and give and take. "I look after Grandpa, and he looks after me," says Mrs. Bowles.
photos.transcriptNote: Transcribed from the cutting. The original says "saws Mrs. Bowles", a printer's slip for "says".

photos.caption: Henry's birth certificate. He was born on 14 June 1894, and his birth was registered in the Glastonbury sub-district of Wells, so he was born in mid-Somerset, not at Stoford. This short copy was issued in 1957.
photos.alt: A red and white printed certificate headed Certificate of Birth, with a royal coat of arms and typed entries. A full transcript follows.
transcript: John Gardiner Woodhouse, Deputy Superintendent Registrar for the Registration District of Wells, compiled from an entry in a register in his custody
photos.transcriptNote: A short birth certificate gives only the name, sex, date and district. The full register entry would also give the exact place of birth and his parents' names.

scenes.title: Yeovil before the war
scenes.intro: Yeovil was a busy market town, famous for one thing above all: gloves.

activities.question: What do we really know about young Henry?
activities.hint: For each fact, choose where our knowledge comes from.

items.text: He was the eldest of twelve children.
items.explain: From Grandma Angela's memoir. A 1953 newspaper cutting the family kept agrees: twelve children, the eldest aged 59, which was Henry.
items.source: Grandma Angela's memoir; newspaper cutting, December 1953

items.explain: It is on his casualty record, which the regimental museum summarised for the family.
He was in France by summer 1915, months before anyone could be made to join, so he must have volunteered.
items.source: His casualty record and medal roll

items.text: He worked as a farm hand.
items.explain: Grandma Angela's memoir describes him on the land, and the photograph on the plough.
From his birth certificate, which the family kept: 14 June 1894.
Not known yet. Most children then left school at 12 to 14 to work.

stories.title: A town of gloves
stories.body: In the 1890s, between 70 and 80 in every 100 people in Yeovil worked in leather, gloving or trades linked to them. Women and girls stitched gloves at home and in the factories.
stories.source: Yeovil's Virtual Museum, Leather and gloving

stories.title: The land and the railway
stories.body: Around the town, families like Henry's lived by farming and the railway. The Bowles family lived right by Yeovil Junction station at Stoford.
stories.source: Somerset Historic Environment Record; Grandma Angela's memoir

stories.title: What we don't know yet
stories.body: We now know Henry's date of birth, 14 June 1894, from his birth certificate, and his parents' names, Arthur and Eliza Ann, from a newspaper cutting. We still don't know his mother's maiden name, exactly where he was born, when the family moved to Stoford, or where he went to school. The full birth register entry and the 1901 and 1911 census should tell us. These are on the family's jobs list.
